judgments.reasoning_cat1: The funding promise is self-cancelling on its face — DMSA "shall contribute the initial capital ... in an amount that DMSA deems appropriate," and the parenthetical lets in-kind items like "the labor of management and staff of DMSA" count as capital, so the size and nature of the obligation is indeterminate; "all expenditures must be done with the concurrence of DMSA" also sits awkwardly against LSB's stated responsibility for "managing the day-to-day operations." The promise that owners "will sign an agreement" on rights of first refusal is an agreement-to-agree, and names/words are misrendered ("Lilhan"/"Lillian", "editonial").
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Paragraph 1 says all distributed profits go "to the members in proportion to their membership interest," while paragraph 4 imposes a waterfall paying out-of-pocket costs and repaying DMSA's initial capital ahead of any proportional distribution, and paragraph 6 contemplates a later operating agreement that could override it. The tax-distribution mandate here is also duplicated as merely the third priority in paragraph 4, leaving the two provisions hard to harmonise.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause first frees DMSA of "any obligation to assign existing, or originate new business ... or any other contracts" — a catch-all after an enumerated list — and then says DMSA "does agree that it intends to use diligent efforts to direct appropriate business to the Company"; "intends to use diligent efforts" and "appropriate business" are precisely the kind of terms two sides read differently. The mirror obligation binds "neither LSB nor its principals," though LSB is an individual with no principals, and shifts to "the Company" where the rest of the paragraph says "the LLC."
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The disclaimer of any duty to bring business to the venture is in real tension with the opening promise in this same paragraph and with paragraph 1's premise that the parties formed the LLC "for the purpose of jointly developing" the Business, and with paragraph 5's confidentiality regime protecting client lists DMSA may keep for itself. The asymmetry — LSB exclusively bound, DMSA free to compete — is the sort of whole-instrument incoherence a court is asked to reconcile.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single undefined sentence: "initially" fixes no period, "rely on the staffs" states no terms, cost allocation or duty, and it is unclear whether it obliges anyone to supply staff at all. It is short and open-textured in the way that invites construction.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: "Dialogo" is the name paragraph 1 gives to the new LLC itself, so referring to the LLC relying on "the staffs of DMSA and Dialogo" is circular unless it means LSB's pre-existing publication — a defined-term mismatch with paragraph 1. It also sits uneasily with paragraph 1's grant to LSB of authority over "recruiting and hiring employees and contractors" and paragraph 4's bar on incurring costs outside an approved budget.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The waterfall applies to "amounts paid to the LLC by clients" — gross receipts, not profits — and the first tier reimburses "any out of pocket costs" without saying whose, while "the approved budget" is a term the document never establishes a mechanism to create. The text is additionally garbled to the point that the final sentence has no ascertainable meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cannot be squared with paragraph 1, which promises that all distributed profits go proportionally to members and that tax-covering cash be distributed each year, whereas here proportional distribution is last and wholly discretionary and DMSA's capital is repaid first. The "approved budget" restriction also cuts against paragraph 1's grant to LSB of day-to-day operational management.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The definition of "Proprietary Information" is a long enumerated list of client, marketing, financial and supplier categories with no general catch-all and no carve-out for information already known or publicly available, so its edges are arguable; the surviving text is legible enough to apply but the consent requirement ("without the prior written consent of the LLC") is loosely expressed. Nothing in it names a term with two plainly competing meanings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It has to coexist with paragraph 2, which lets DMSA and its principals retain and originate advertising contracts and clients for their own benefit — arguably the same client lists and prospects the definition captures — but the two can be read together without contradiction. No other provision addresses confidentiality, and no duration or survival term elsewhere conflicts with it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It commits the parties to execute articles of organization and an operating agreement "with ... standard terms and conditions" — an undefined standard that leaves the content of the essential documents to be agreed later, the classic agreement-to-agree. The duplicated "execute execute" and the badly rendered text add to the uncertainty about what documents are covered.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with paragraph 1's separate promise that the owners "will sign an agreement" on rights of first refusal and additional interests, this raises whether the venture agreement is itself the operative bargain or only a step toward one — a whole-instrument question about enforceability. The contemplated operating agreement could also displace paragraphs 1 and 4's distribution and governance terms without any stated priority rule.
